column4: People are warned of a day when they will be returned to God and every soul will be paid in full for what it earned; return and account are stated as one sequence.
After rescue, people transgress during the brief enjoyment of the nearer life; then their return is to God and He informs them of their deeds, closely matching the section's sequence.
God grants a wrongdoing town respite, then seizes it, and to Him is the destination; delay cannot change where the reprieved finally arrives.
A town that defiantly turned from its Lord's command and messengers was called to a severe account, joining refusal directly to reckoning.
The town of 65:8 tastes the evil result of its conduct and ends in loss, supplying the consequence of its severe account.
Corruption is made manifest so people may taste part of what they have done “that they may return”; a nearer consequence is again an opening for voluntary return.
Pharaoh's people are seized with punishment so that they might return, another direct instance of preliminary punishment serving return before the end.
The Children of Israel are tested with both good things and evil things so that they might return; the good-and-evil polarity serves voluntary return rather than fixing the final destination.
People of the Book are warned to believe before faces are effaced and turned back upon their backs; face, reversal, and threatened judgment meet in one image.
Everything perishes except God's face, judgment belongs to Him, and to Him people are returned; face, account, and destination converge explicitly.
The change of qiblah distinguishes one who follows the Messenger from one who turns back on his heels; literal direction exposes moral reversal.
After the Messenger's death, whoever turns back on his heels cannot harm God; departure changes the person, not the divine end or authority.
Obedience is commanded, but if people turn away the Messenger's obligation is only clear delivery, another exact formulation of the reminder's bounded role.
When the one God is mentioned in the Quran, the hearers turn their backs in aversion; moral refusal is staged as the bodily back-turning developed by the section.
The person reminded of the Lord's signs then turns away and forgets what his hands sent ahead; present refusal is inseparable from the deeds awaiting account.
Whoever turns away from God's reminder will carry a burden on Resurrection Day, directly joining rejection of reminder to the final consequence.
The turner of 20:100 remains under that burden, which is an evil load on Resurrection Day; this gives the enduring outcome of the refusal.
Whoever turns from God's reminder receives a constricted life and is raised blind on Resurrection Day; worldly orientation issues in the condition of return.
No one is more unjust than the person reminded of the Lord's signs who then turns away; divine retribution follows the rejected reminder.
The Quran gives good news and warning, yet most turn away and do not hear; it stages the failed reception of the prophetic reminder.
Whoever turns from the Lord's reminder is made to enter mounting punishment, attaching aversion from remembrance to its destination.
After considering the revelation, the opponent turns his back and acts arrogantly; the bodily turn is the decisive movement toward the punishment later named in the passage.
Pharaoh denies and disobeys, supplying the moral content of the turn described in the next ayah.
Pharaoh then turns his back and strives, an enacted departure whose destination is the divine seizure in 79:25.
God seizes Pharaoh with an exemplary punishment for the last and first offenses, completing the path begun by his back-turning in 79:22.
The opponents are asked whether the news of earlier peoples has not come to them; the arrival of report carries warning through remembered outcomes.
Messengers ask earlier nations whether the news of those before them has not come, another direct scene in which news arrives to its hearers.
The news of former disbelievers is asked as something that came to the hearers, and that news includes the evil consequence they tasted.
Earlier peoples denied, so punishment came upon them from where they did not perceive; unseen arrival realizes the threat carried by غاشية.
Plotters are asked whether they feel secure from punishment coming from where they do not perceive, preserving the image of unnoticed threatening arrival.
Hell has a bed beneath its people and coverings above them; the plural غَوَاشٍ makes punitive envelopment a complete surrounding scene.
The favorable recipient is given his record in his right hand, identifying the person whose return proceeds to the easy account in 84:8.
The recipient of the record behind his back calls for destruction, beginning the consequence of the backward-facing account scene.
He enters a blazing fire, completing the destination attached to the record delivered behind his back.
After denying and turning away, the person goes back to his family swaggering; apparent departure toward home occurs inside a passage that says the driving is to the Lord.
The tranquil soul is addressed before being commanded to return, identifying the inward state capable of the willing return in 89:28.
After returning contentedly, the soul is told to enter among God's servants, specifying the company into which that return leads.
The returning soul is told to enter God's garden, completing the favorable destination of the voluntary return.
Even amid parental pressure toward association, the servant is told that the return is to God and He will inform everyone of their deeds; allegiance ends in disclosure.
After the warning not to obey parents in association, God says that to Him is the return and He will inform people of what they did.
Those struck by affliction confess that they belong to God and are returning to Him; recognition freely anticipates the universal return.
Believers give what they give while their hearts fear because they are returning to their Lord; awareness of return already directs present action.
The believer states that everyone's return is to God and that the transgressors are companions of the Fire, joining common return to divergent receptions.
God raises everyone, informs them of their deeds, and has counted what they forgot; resurrection culminates in exact disclosure and account.
The record is placed, wrongdoers fear its contents, and nothing small or great is omitted; this expands what “upon Us is their account” entails.
On that Day every soul is repaid for what it earned, without injustice, and God is swift in account; it states the character of the reckoning after return.
Every community is seen kneeling and summoned to its record, staging the posture and documentary summons of final account.
God's record speaks truth and preserves what people did, explaining the evidentiary basis of the account in 45:28.
Deniers of meeting God regret when the Hour comes suddenly and carry their burdens, joining unforeseen arrival to the denied meeting.
Death overtakes people wherever they are, even in fortified towers; no chosen place or direction prevents the decisive arrival.
At death the angels strike disbelievers' faces and backs, bringing the section's opposed bodily sides together at the beginning of return.
When angels take the disbelievers in death, they strike their faces and backs; the gesture of refusal is overtaken at the boundary of return.
With humbled eyes people emerge from graves and move toward the caller, a compulsory bodily response on the Day of return.
Their eyes are humbled and abasement covers them, though in life they were called to prostrate while able; final posture answers earlier refusal.
They rush from graves with humbled eyes while abasement covers them, realizing the Day they had been promised.
Eyes are humbled amid the resurrection terror, closely echoing the humbled faces at the opening of surah 88's judgment scene.
Followers under punishment wish for another return so they might disown their leaders; the desired return exists only as regret once the consequences appear.
When the Book's outcome arrives, deniers ask for intercession or a return so they can act differently; realized judgment closes the former choice.
The condemned wish for another turn so they could become believers, defining compulsory arrival as the point beyond which willing return is unavailable.
When death comes, a soul asks for a short delay to give and become righteous; the appeal reveals a return to action sought too late.
God will not delay a soul once its appointed time comes, closing the requested interval of 63:10.
The Prophet is commanded to turn away from them until the caller summons people to something terrible; here prophetic withdrawal awaits their compulsory response.
Those who turn back on their heels after guidance is clear are enticed and given false hopes; their backward motion is a chosen reversal after recognition.
Those God leaves astray are gathered on their faces toward Hell, so the face that once chose orientation becomes the surface of compulsory movement.
Faces are turned about in the Fire while their owners regret obeying leaders rather than the Messenger; final facial motion exposes misdirected allegiance.
Criminals are dragged on their faces into the Fire, making the final direction imposed rather than chosen.
God makes night cover day as each rapidly pursues the other, a repeated natural instance of the enveloping sense of غ ش و.
Night covering day is repeated in a creation context, preserving the ordinary covering sense beside the idiom of a coming affliction.
Moses warns his people not to turn back on their backs lest they become losers; retreat is pictured as bodily reversal from a commanded destination.
Moses turns and flees without looking back when the staff moves, a literal fear-driven use of the bodily turn that differs from culpable aversion.
The same staff scene again has Moses turn and flee without returning, confirming the literal motion sense and its nonmoral context.
People fold their breasts and cover themselves to hide, yet God knows what they conceal and reveal; turning and covering fail to escape divine knowledge before account.
